title: Why the people chose Rama
hookLine: the second book opens with an old king asking a hall full of people: why Rama?
carry: Rama is dharma in human form

lines: BARK CLOTHES AND A FOREST: THE END.
cards: Many people know how the second book of the Ramayana ends: a prince in clothes made of bark, walking into the forest with his wife and his brother. So notice how the Ayodhya Kanda begins. Not with a villain.

Not with a quarrel. With an old man who loves his son, and a room full of people who love him too. For the next few weeks, almost everything turns on one family's household, and the first thing in it is good news.

teach.h: ONE KINDNESS KEPT, A HUNDRED WRONGS NOT.
teach.b: Dasharatha has ruled a long time, and he feels it. Rama is the one the whole city talks about. Valmiki pauses to describe him, and one detail stands out.
If someone does Rama a single kindness, he is pleased by it. If someone does him a hundred wrongs, he doesn't keep count.
So the king makes a plan.
He'll name Rama the yuvaraja, the young king, the heir who shares the rule while his father is still alive. He doesn't simply announce it.

He calls an assembly: counselors, leading citizens, kings from the lands around, though in his hurry, the text notes, he doesn't send for Janaka or for Bharata's grandfather in Kekaya. If you agree, tell me.
If there's a better course, tell me that too. The hall answers with one roar of yes. And the old king tests them: why Rama, while I'm still ruling well?
So they tell him. His truthfulness, his courage, his kindness to ordinary people, how he asks after their families and their fields. Here's why this matters to Hindus.
Rama is God come down, but the Ramayana keeps showing him as a person you could actually follow.

teach.h: RAMA IS DHARMA WITH A BODY.
teach.b: Later in the epic, even an enemy, the demon Maricha, says it plainly: Rama is dharma with a body.

That's why grandparents still hold him up to children, and call him maryada purushottam, the best of persons, who keeps within dharma's bounds. Perfect in how he lived it: truthful, kind, a hundred wrongs not counted.
And that's why what happens next will hurt so much.

how: Many Hindu families read the Ayodhya Kanda as the heart of the Ramayana. Rama is often called maryada purushottam, the best of persons who keeps within the bounds of dharma, and his habit of remembering kindness and forgetting wrongs is often held up as a model for children.

s: Dasharatha decides on Rama's coronation alone
he calls an assembly and asks it, and they answer gladly.
the Ayodhya Kanda opens with good news
an old king's plan to share the throne with his eldest son.
Hindus call Rama ideal because nothing was ever hard for him
the story keeps testing him; he's held up for how he lives dharma, as 'dharma with a body'.

games.q: you're Dasharatha, old and tired, ready to share the throne. how do you do it?
o: ask an assembly whether they agree.
games.why: he asks the assembly, invites them to propose a better course, and even tests them: why Rama? they answer with his virtues.

practice: Rama kept one kindness and let a hundred wrongs go uncounted. Bring to mind one kindness someone did for you this year, and let it be vivid: the place, the face. If you pray, offer a quiet thank-you for that person, by name.
If a hurt from the same person crowds in, let it sit further back for now, and spend the rest of the sit with the kindness.

wordCard.voice: Yuvaraja, the young king who shares the rule while his father still reigns. Dasharatha proposes Rama for the title, and asks his assembly, which answers with joy.

orig.note: Sanskrit yuvarāja: young king. the heir named while the father still reigns, the title Dasharatha means to give Rama.

carryVoice: Your line: Rama is dharma in human form. One kindness kept, a hundred wrongs let go. See you tomorrow.
